label: Claude Fable 5.2
output:
**The house in Glenmore**

I have news about the house in Glenmore, and I want every one of you to have it from me, in the same words, on the same day. Some of you have it already and didn't get it from me. I'll come to that, because it's the part I handled badly.

I have agreed to sell the house. The sale was agreed on Tuesday the 3rd of November, and it closes on Friday the 15th of January 2027. I'm putting the date here near the top so that nobody is left to hear it from somebody else.

For the younger ones in Boston and Perth and Leeds, who may know it mostly from photographs, this is the old Mulkerrin place outside Oughterard. Tom's grandfather, Pádraig Mulkerrin, built it in 1931, and Tom grew up in it. That is ninety-five years in the one family. I know well what I'm signing away, and I didn't come to it quickly, however sudden it may have looked to anyone who got the news in a text message.

First, how you heard. I meant to tell each of you myself, and I was too slow about it, and the news went round without me. Several of you got it second-hand, on the phone or on WhatsApp, in bits and with half the facts missing. That is my own fault and nobody else's. You should have heard it from me and you didn't, and I'm sorry.

I want to be careful about what I'm sorry for, though. I'm sorry for the way you found out. I am not sorry for the decision, and I'd be telling you a lie if I said I was. So here is the whole of it, the hard parts included, and you can make up your own minds about me afterwards.

Since Tom died in March 2024 I have driven out to Glenmore every fortnight. It's forty minutes each way. I open the windows to air the rooms, I check the pipes, and then I lock up and drive home again. I have done that in all weathers for more than two and a half years. I did it gladly at the start, because it felt like minding something for him. But you can't keep a house by visiting it. All I have been doing is watching it go downhill, a fortnight at a time.

In September I got Ó Flaithearta's out to survey the roof. The slates need doing and so does the back chimney, and the quote came to €38,000. That doesn't cover the damp in the back bedroom, which is a job of its own. Then there's the septic tank, which needs replacing, and that has to be done before the house could be sold to anybody at all. There was no way around that one, whatever I decided.

I'm giving you the figures because you're entitled to them, and because I'd rather you had them from me than a rounded-up version from somebody else. The house needs a great deal of money and a great deal of minding, and it needs them from someone who is in it every day. I can't go on maintaining it. I have turned that sentence around every way I know how and it comes out the same each time.

Now for something I've told nobody.

Last February, in the frost, I slipped on the step at the back door. I lay there for twenty minutes before I could get up. There was nobody to call to, and nobody due. I got up in the end, and I said nothing about it to anyone, not that day and not since. You are all reading it here for the first time, and I can see now that keeping it to myself was foolish.

I have been afraid to be alone at that house ever since. I don't enjoy writing that down. I spent my working life telling small children there was nothing to be afraid of, and here I am at 71, nervous of a back step. But it's true, and it's a big part of the reason, and I said I'd give you all of it. Every fortnight since then I've stood at that door with the key in my hand and thought about how long I might be lying there the next time.

So that is the why of it. The roof, the cost, the drive, and the fact that I'm frightened out there by myself.

Now, who is buying it. Their names are Aoife and Kevin Joyce. They're a young couple with two small children, and Kevin is from Maam Cross, so he isn't coming far. They want to live in it. They are not buying it as a holiday let. They told me that straight, and I believe them.

The price was fair. It was also less than I was offered in the summer by the Dublin crowd, and I want you to know that I took the lower offer on purpose. I'd sooner you knew that than found it out later and wondered. If anyone thinks it was a foolish thing to do, you're welcome to tell me so and I'll listen, but I'd do the same again tomorrow.

Tom always said that house should have children in it and not be a museum. I heard it often enough that I can hear it yet. If I had held on, a museum is exactly what it would have become, and a leaking one, with me as the caretaker calling once a fortnight to open the windows. Instead there will be two small children growing up in it, with a father from over the road in Maam Cross. I think Tom would have picked the Joyces over the Dublin crowd himself, and I think he'd have taken less money to do it.

It has taken me the best part of two years to see that I can keep Tom's memory without keeping the house. I didn't believe that at the start. For a long while the two were the same thing in my mind, and driving out to air the rooms was the nearest I could get to calling on him. I don't feel that any more. He's as much with me at my own kitchen table as he ever was in Glenmore, and some days more.

He proposed to me in the haggard behind that house in 1979. It was raining, and the cattle stood and watched the whole thing. The children learned to swim in the lake below the house, and Declan would refuse to come out of the water until his lips were blue. I will have all of that for as long as I have my wits, and it doesn't go to the Joyces with the keys.

Here is what's staying in the family. The dresser is going to Úna's. Pádraig's fiddle is being kept, and so are the photographs, every one of them. The Sacred Heart lamp is coming out of the house with us, and the sign is coming off the gate. Those things were never going to be sold along with it. If you were lying awake wondering about any of them, you can stop.

The Joyces have also said that the family can come out and walk the land any time. I'd ask you to hold them to it. If you're home next summer, or the summer after, go out and introduce yourself and walk down to the lake. They know who we are and what the place is to us.

There is one person I have to speak to directly, and I'd sooner do it here in front of everyone than have people guessing.

Declan heard about the sale from his cousin Gráinne, in a WhatsApp message. That is no fault of Gráinne's. It's mine. He rang me at two in the morning his time, and he told me I was selling Dad. I said things back to him that I shouldn't have said. I won't write them here. He knows what they were and so do I.

Declan, I know you read these. I'm not angry with you. I was hurt that night and I let it come out as temper, and I'm sorry for what I said. You had every right to be upset. You found out about your father's home from a phone screen, when your own mother should have rung you before anyone. I'd have been raging too.

I should have talked to you before I agreed to anything. I didn't, and I regret it, and I expect I'll go on regretting it. But I have to be straight with you as well. I'm not willing to wait until you're home in the summer. The roof won't hold off until then and neither, if I'm honest, will my nerve. You've read above about the step and the frost. I can't face another year of going out there by myself, and I won't ask the Joyces to hang on for months on the chance that we'd all feel better about it by then.

I am not selling your father. I couldn't if I tried. But I understand why it sounded like that at two in the morning, and I'd like the chance to talk about it properly, whenever suits you. The door is open and the phone is on. Ring at any hour, yours or mine.

Now, the last thing, and a happier one.

Before the house is cleared I'd like us to have a day in it. Sunday the 13th of December, out at the house, for anyone who can come. There'll be soup and sandwiches. Bring wellies, because the ground will be soft and I'd like people to be able to go down to the lake and around the fields without ruining their good shoes. I'll put a time up here closer to the day. Let me know if you're coming, so I have some idea how much soup to make.

There's no programme. Walk through the rooms, look at the photographs before they're packed, stand in the haggard if you like, though I can't promise you cattle. Bring the children. If they run through the house and make noise in it, so much the better.

I know a Sunday in December outside Oughterard is no use to most of you in Boston and Perth, and it may not be much use to Leeds either. I'm sorry about that. The timing is tight and there was no date that would have suited everyone. The Joyces' offer is there for you whenever you are home, and I'll go out with you myself if you'd like the company.

So that's everything I have. The sale was agreed on the 3rd of November, the day at the house is Sunday the 13th of December, and it closes on Friday the 15th of January. If you have a question, ask me and not each other. If you're cross with me, tell me that too. I'd rather have it to my face than hear it on the grapevine, having put the rest of you through exactly that.

With love to every one of you,

A few things to check before you post:

- **Your name:** I left the sign-off blank because I don't know what the family calls you.
- **Time for the 13th:** you didn't give one, so the post says you'll put it up nearer the day. Swap in a time if you have one.
- **Days of the week:** I added Tuesday for 3 November and Friday for 15 January from the calendar.
- **Small things I filled in:** a few lines are my guesses at how you felt, such as the early drives feeling like minding the house for Tom, and calling the fall "foolish" to have kept quiet. I also had you offer to go out to the house with visiting cousins. Change or cut anything that isn't true to you.
